clusters.headline: US Stocks Decline, Led by Tech Sector Sell-Off on October 16
clusters.briefing: US stock markets experienced declines on Friday, October 16, with a broad sell-off in technology companies contributing to the S&P 500 and Nasdaq recording their worst week since late June. The Nasdaq declined approximately 2.3% on Friday, while the S&P 500 fell by 1.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55%. The S&P 500 closed at 7,649.71 points, the Nasdaq at 26,128.13 points, and the Dow at 51,891.77 points. Selling extended beyond chipmakers to include AI infrastructure, cloud computing, and cybersecurity companies. Some individual tech stocks experienced steeper losses than the broader equity indices. European stocks, however, finished higher on Friday and posted weekly gains.

articles.title: S&P 500 analysis and forecast after the "AI bubble" panic
articles.description:
S&P 500 forecast after the AI bubble panic: Why Friday's selloff is not yet a major bearish reversal

Friday's selloff in AI and chip stocks looked alarming, but the S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) are telling a somewhat less frightening story. Following the October 16 close, my four-hour technical analysis still shows a decline within a broader trading range, rather than a confirmed major bearish trend reversal. The next important test is around 7,668, and I explain why in my video below:

AI stocks were hit hard, but the broader market tells a different story

For investors holding semiconductor and AI-related stocks, Friday was certainly an uncomfortable day.

As Adam Button reported in AI names fall as the Nasdaq comes under fresh pressure, selling extended beyond chipmakers into AI infrastructure, cloud computing and cybersecurity companies. Some individual stocks suffered much steeper losses than the broader equity indices.

The investingLive Americas market wrap showed the Nasdaq down approximately 2.3% on Friday, compared with a 1.2% decline in the S&P 500.

That difference is worth paying attention to.

A sharp decline in popular technology stocks can create the impression that the entire stock market is entering a major collapse. However, weakness in market leaders does not necessarily mean that the broader market has already confirmed a bearish reversal.

We also saw a different picture internationally. European stocks finished higher on Friday and posted weekly gains, illustrating how unevenly the selling pressure was distributed.

This does not make the risks in AI stocks disappear. It simply suggests that we should distinguish between a sharp sector selloff and a confirmed breakdown in the broader stock market.

And that brings me to the S&P 500 chart.

Watch my S&P 500 futures technical analysis and forecast in the video below. I explain the trading range, the price channel and the conditions that would make me considerably more bearish.

Why the S&P 500 still looks like a trading range

The central observation in my analysis is that ES remains within a recognizable trading range.

On the four-hour chart, price has been moving through alternating advances and declines, with sellers taking control near resistance and buyers responding around support.

I also identify a price channel that has helped frame these movements since September. The channel's boundaries and midpoint have repeatedly interacted with price, including around the latest decline.

In particular, the recent selling followed a rejection near two overlapping resistance references: the channel's midpoint and the upper boundary of the range's value area.

The value area is the price region where roughly 70% of the trading volume occurred over the period being examined. Its upper and lower boundaries can help identify where the market has previously accepted substantial trading activity.

After failing near resistance, ES moved back toward the lower boundary of that value area.

This brings us to an especially interesting part of Friday's price action.

S&P 500 futures: Why 7,668 matters

Around 7,668, several technical references come together.

First, this is approximately the lower boundary of the value area for the range examined in the video.

Second, the October 16 decline approached the lower boundary of the price channel.

Third, the market was revisiting a support region associated with earlier lows around September 18 and October 1.

These are three different reasons why traders might pay attention to approximately the same area.

For example, some short sellers may decide to take profits when price reaches established support. Other traders may consider a speculative long position, while traders following the channel could view the lower boundary as an area where a rebound becomes possible.

I am not claiming to know which participants were buying or covering shorts on Friday. The observation is that price reached an area where several recognizable support references converged.

The important point is that Friday's decline had not yet produced the sustained breakdown below this area that I would want to see before interpreting the move as a more significant bearish development.

That does not mean support must hold on the next test. It means the market has not yet provided sufficient evidence for my more bearish scenario.

What would turn the S&P 500 outlook more bearish?

This is where my forecast becomes conditional.

In my opinion, the more meaningful warning would be two or three consecutive completed four-hour candles closing below approximately 7,668.

Why not simply react to the first move below that level?

Because markets frequently cross support or resistance briefly before reversing direction. A momentary break can reflect a liquidity event or a failed attempt to establish a new trading range.

Several consecutive closes below support would provide stronger evidence that sellers are establishing acceptance at lower prices, rather than merely pushing the market temporarily beyond a familiar boundary.

An additional development worth watching would be a subsequent recovery attempt that fails to reclaim the broken support.

For example, if ES breaks below 7,668, rebounds toward that area, encounters renewed selling and then continues lower, the bearish interpretation becomes more credible.

Even then, a downside break would not automatically establish a long-term bear market. It would first signal that the current trading range is potentially resolving lower, with the wider trend requiring further evaluation.

And what if S&P 500 support holds?

The alternative is that buyers continue defending the existing support region.

If ES holds around 7,668 and begins recovering, the next question becomes whether price can reclaim the channel's midpoint and challenge the higher-volume resistance region that previously attracted selling.

Such a recovery would fit the existing trading-range interpretation.

However, I would be careful about declaring a new bullish breakout simply because the market rebounds from support.

There is an important difference between a recovery within a range and a sustained move out of that range.

A rebound could improve the immediate technical picture while leaving the broader market in consolidation.

For now, I am not automatically bullish or bearish. My interpretation is that the recent weakness is meaningful, but the evidence for a major bearish reversal remains incomplete.

The next catalysts: Technology earnings, inflation and the Federal Reserve

Technical support is only part of the picture.

Investors also need to consider what could change market sentiment as trading resumes.

The upcoming earnings calendar could be particularly important for determining whether AI-related selling remains concentrated in certain stocks or spreads further across the market.

As discussed in Earnings week ahead: Banks were upbeat on the economy, now onto tech, the latest bank results suggested that important parts of the US economy remain resilient. The next earnings announcements will provide another opportunity to evaluate how businesses are navigating current conditions.

Meanwhile, inflation, energy prices and monetary policy remain potential sources of volatility.

Giuseppe Dellamotta's review of changing interest-rate expectations illustrates how traders are reassessing the Federal Reserve outlook amid persistent inflation concerns.

One reason this matters for stocks is that higher costs do not necessarily translate into higher corporate profits. Justin Low offers a useful explanation in Why higher inflation doesn't always mean bigger corporate profits.

These macroeconomic concerns also formed part of my earlier Dow Jones futures analysis for October 16, although that analysis reflected an earlier market snapshot before Friday's selling intensified.

Taken together, the question for the coming week is whether disappointing developments cause the broader indices to break established support, or whether the latest weakness remains largely a correction within existing trading structures.

My S&P 500 forecast: Respect the selling, but wait for confirmation

My main takeaway after reviewing Friday's price action is straightforward.

The selling pressure is real, particularly in technology stocks, but the S&P 500 futures chart is not yet confirming the kind of major bearish trend reversal that some investors may fear.

The market has reached an important support region, and the next reaction around 7,668 could provide useful information.

Holding that region would keep the existing trading-range interpretation intact. Sustained four-hour closes below it, particularly followed by a failed recovery, would make me reassess the bearish risks more seriously.

The market could certainly move lower. I am not ruling that out.

But there is a difference between anticipating a major reversal and having sufficient evidence that one is actually developing.

For traders and investors, recognizing that difference can help avoid making decisions based purely on frightening headlines or the latest sharp move in a few popular stocks.

S&P 500 forecast on a wider perspective (the simple weekly chart)

I typically perform some heavy and sophisticated analysis with lots of data but for traders and investors at investingLive.com, I like to simplify and show them the simple charts. Less is more for many of our readers. That is where apx 7600 (shown as 7,608.89 below) comes in, if S&P 500 decides to sell some more. 

S&P 500 futures: The weekly 20 EMA in my above simple chart could become an important support test

S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) remain in a broader uptrend on the weekly chart, although the latest pullback suggests buyers are facing renewed pressure near the highs.

During the week ending October 16, futures approached the previous week's high near 7,900, but failed to extend the rally. The contract subsequently declined to close around 7,703, a weekly loss of approximately 2.1%.

Despite this weakness, the broader bullish structure has not yet been decisively undermined.

The first area to watch is around 7,670-7,680. The latest weekly low near 7,676 almost matched the late-September low around 7,673, making this an immediate reference area for potential stabilization.

Further below, the 20-week exponential moving average (EMA), currently around 7,609, could become an important support reference if the decline continues.

This moving average has been rising alongside the broader advance. However, price has not yet tested it during the latest pullback, so its ability to attract renewed buying interest remains unproven.

A decline toward the EMA followed by a convincing weekly rebound would support the interpretation that the market is experiencing a correction within a continuing uptrend.

Conversely, a completed weekly close below the moving average, followed by an unsuccessful attempt to recover it, would suggest that the correction may be developing into something more significant. The early-September lows around 7,575-7,585 provide another nearby structural reference.

On the upside, a sustained recovery toward 7,850-7,900 would help restore the bullish case.

The takeaway: The weekly 20 EMA offers a potentially useful future support test, but the more important evidence will be how prices behave if they reach it. A moving average identifies an area worth watching, not a guarantee that buyers will defend it.

This analysis reflects the October 16, 2026 market close and is my technical interpretation as of October 17. It is educational commentary, not financial advice.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

clusters.briefing: Substantial investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure are evident, with AI proving beneficial for productivity and expansion across various industries. However, rising borrowing costs are signaling funding risks for global AI expansion, according to a Jefferies report. Companies such as Oracle and CoreWeave are facing heightened credit risk due to struggles with borrowing. One strategist notes that the AI trade has not been immune to rising bond yields. Gary Marcus warned that the demise of leading AI firms could trigger extensive financial repercussions, comparing a potential AI bubble burst to a 2008-like banking crisis and raising flags about OpenAI's fiscal responsibilities. Morgan Stanley, however, backs global stocks over bonds, citing strong economic growth and rising corporate profits boosting risk assets, while flagging an oil shock as a risk.

clusters.headline: Brent crude oil reaches $110 per barrel, a five-month high
clusters.briefing: Brent crude oil prices reached $110 per barrel on October 16, marking the first time since May that the international benchmark has hit this level. Oil prices have been above $100 a barrel for most of the past month. This increase is attributed to geopolitical risks, including the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war, which have created persistent shocks for the industry. Reports of Saudi Arabia-led forces intercepting missiles aimed at critical energy hubs also contributed to the price jump. Diesel and gasoline futures also climbed as traders assessed disrupted energy infrastructure and limited prospects for immediate supply relief. Additionally, the physical delivery cost of oil has increased, with tanker rates surging, adding approximately $38 per barrel to the cost.

clusters.headline: Central Bank of India Q2 net profit rises 21% to ₹1,469 crore
clusters.briefing: Central Bank of India reported a 21% increase in net profit for the September 2026 quarter, reaching ₹1,469 crore. This was supported by a 26% growth in net interest income to ₹4,146 crore and a 30% expansion in total advances to ₹3.81 lakh crore. Interest income rose 18.45% year-over-year to ₹10,357 crore, with interest earned on advances increasing 27.6% to ₹7,231 crore. The bank's asset quality improved, with net non-performing assets declining to 0.31%. In contrast, IDBI Bank's Q2 FY27 net profit decreased 39% year-on-year to ₹2,205 crore, though excluding a one-off gain from the previous year, profit rose 14%. IDBI Bank's deposits grew 17% and advances increased 18%. ICICI Bank's net interest margin fell to 4.18% in the September quarter from 4.36% in the June quarter. Separately, Ixigo reported a consolidated net profit of ₹63.42 crore for the September quarter, recovering from a net loss of ₹3.46 crore in the prior year.

clusters.briefing: The US federal government's budget deficit for fiscal year 2026 totaled $1.992 trillion, marking the seventh consecutive year the deficit has exceeded a trillion dollars. Household debt grew at an annual rate of 4.1 percent in Q3 2025, with consumer credit up 2.3 percent and mortgage debt up 3.2 percent. Household percent equity in real estate was 71.6% in Q3 2025, a decrease from 72.0% in Q2 2025.

clusters.briefing: The U.S. goods and services deficit was $29.4 billion in October, a decrease of $18.8 billion from the revised September figure of $48.1 billion. October exports totaled $302.0 billion, an increase of $7.8 billion from September, and were up 12% year-over-year. October imports were $331.4 billion, a decrease of $11.0 billion from September, and were down 4% year-over-year. The trade deficit with China decreased to $14.9 billion from $28.1 billion a year prior. Separately, in the 12 months ending in September, export prices advanced to almost 12 percent, marking the highest increase in over four years. Wholesale prices, as measured by the producer price index, climbed 1.3% in September and increased 6.3% annually, which is the largest gain since 2022.

clusters.headline: Comments on December Employment Report
clusters.briefing:
- Comments on December Employment Report — The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000. The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

Earlier: December Employment Report: 50 thousand Jobs, 4.4% Unemployment Rate

Prime (25 to 54 Years Old) Participation

Since the overall participation rate is impacted by both cyclical (recession) and demographic (aging population, younger people staying in school) reasons, here is the employment-population ratio for the key working age group: 25 to 54 years old.

The 25 to 54 years old participation rate was unchanged in December at 83.8%% from 83.8% in November.

The 25 to 54 employment population ratio increased to 80.7% from 80.6% the previous month.

Both are down slightly from the recent peaks, but still near the highest level this millennium.

Average Hourly Wages

The graph shows the nominal year-over-year change in "Average Hourly Earnings" for all private employees from the Current Employment Statistics (CES).  

There was a huge increase at the beginning of the pandemic as lower paid employees were let go, and then the pandemic related spike reversed a year later.

Wage growth has trended down after peaking at 5.9% YoY in March 2022 and was at 3.8% YoY in December, up from 3.6% YoY in November. 

Part Time for Economic Reasons

From the BLS report:
"The number of people employed part time for economic reasons, at 5.3 million, changed little in December but is up by 980,000 over the year. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs."
The number of persons working part time for economic reasons decreased in December to 5.34 million from 5.49 million in November.  This is well above the pre-pandemic levels and near the highest levels since mid-2021.

These workers are included in the alternate measure of labor underutilization (U-6) that decreased to 8.4% from 8.7% in November. This is down from the record high in April 2020 of 22.9% and up from the lowest level on record (seasonally adjusted) in December 2022 (6.6%). (This series started in 1994). This measure is well above the 7.0% level in February 2020 (pre-pandemic).

Unemployed over 26 Weeks

This graph shows the number of workers unemployed for 27 weeks or more.

According to the BLS, there are 1.95 million workers who have been unemployed for more than 26 weeks and still want a job, up from 1.91 million in November.

This is down from post-pandemic high of 4.171 million, and up from the recent low of 1.056 million.

This is above pre-pandemic levels.

Summary:

The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000.  The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

This was another weak employment report.  
- December Employment Report: 50 thousand Jobs, 4.4% Unemployment Rate — From the BLS: Employment Situation
Both total nonfarm payroll employment (+50,000) and the unemployment rate (4.4 percent) changed little in December, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment continued to trend up in food services and drinking places, health care, and social assistance. Retail trade lost jobs.
...
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for October was revised down by 68,000, from -105,000 to -173,000, and the change for November was revised down by 8,000, from +64,000 to +56,000. With these revisions, employment in October and November combined is 76,000 lower than previously reported.
emphasis added
Click on graph for larger image.

The first graph shows the jobs added per month since January 2021.

Total payrolls increased by 50 thousand in December.  Private payrolls increased by37 thousand, and public payrolls increased 13 thousand.

Payrolls for October and November were revised down by 76 thousand, combined.  The economy has only added 93 thousand jobs since April (8 months).

The second graph shows the year-over-year change in total non-farm employment since 1968.

In December, the year-over-year change was 0.594 million jobs.  

Year-over-year employment growth has slowed sharply.



The third graph shows the employment population ratio and the participation rate.

The Labor Force Participation Rate decreased to 62.4% in December, from 62.5% in November. This is the percentage of the working age population in the labor force.

The Employment-Population ratio increased to 59.7% from 59.6% in November (blue line).

I'll post the 25 to 54 age group employment-population ratio graph later.



The fourth graph shows the unemployment rate.

The unemployment rate was decreased to 4.4% in December from 4.5% in November.  

This was slightly below consensus expectations, however, October and November payrolls were revised down by 76,000 combined.

Overall another weak report.

I'll have more later ...
- December Employment Preview — On Friday at 8:30 AM ET, the BLS will release the employment report for December. The consensus is for 55,000 jobs added, and for the unemployment rate to decrease to 4.5%. There were 64,000 jobs added in November, and the unemployment rate was at 4.6%.

From Goldman Sachs:
We forecast that payrolls rose 70k (vs. 55k consensus) in December and the unemployment rate fell to 4.5% (vs. 4.5% consensus). ... We expect the unemployment rate to edge down to 4.5% because the increase to 4.6% in November largely reflected the impact of furloughed federal government workers during the shutdown.
emphasis added
From BofA:
Dec NFP are likely to tick up to a stable 70k (private: 75k) print, higher than consensus expectations. Initial claims remain low and continuing claims have trended lower since Oct. Education & health jobs should remain the driver of payroll growth. Given the strength in air travel and holiday spending, we project a rise in leisure & hospitality jobs. After the u-rate jumping to 4.6% in Nov, in part due to shutdown-related distortions, we expect a decline to 4.5%. It is likely that the worst is behind us in the labor market.
• ADP Report: The ADP employment report showed 41,000 private sector jobs were added in December.  This was slightly below consensus forecasts.  However, in general, ADP hasn't been very useful in forecasting the BLS report.

• ISM Surveys: Note that the ISM indexes are diffusion indexes based on the number of firms hiring (not the number of hires).  The ISM® manufacturing employment index increased to 44.9%, up from 44.0% the previous month. This suggests manufacturing jobs lost in December. The ADP report indicated 5,000 manufacturing jobs lost in December.

The ISM® services employment index increased to 52.0%, up from 48.9%.  This suggests job gains in December.  

• Unemployment Claims: The weekly claims report showed about the same number of initial unemployment claims during the reference week at 224,000 in December compared to 222,000 in November.  This suggests about the same number of layoffs in December as in November.

• Conclusion: Over the last 6 months, employment gains averaged 17 thousand per month.  The ADP report, the ISM Surveys, and unemployment claims suggest similar gains in December compared to November.   I'll take the over for December - but still weak hiring.
- Weekly Initial Unemployment Claims Increase to 208,000 — The DOL reported:
In the week ending January 3, the advance figure for seasonally adjusted initial claims was 208,000, an increase of 8,000 from the previous week's revised level. The previous week's level was revised up by 1,000 from 199,000 to 200,000. The 4-week moving average was 211,750, a decrease of 7,250 from the previous week's revised average. This is the lowest level for this average since April 27, 2024 when it was 210,250. The previous week's average was revised up by 250 from 218,750 to 219,000.
emphasis added
The following graph shows the 4-week moving average of weekly claims since 1971.

Click on graph for larger image.

The dashed line on the graph is the current 4-week average. The four-week average of weekly unemployment claims decreased to 211,750.

This was slightly above the consensus estimate. - BLS: Job Openings Declined to 7.1 million in November — From the BLS: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Summary
The number of job openings was little changed at 7.1 million in November, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Over the month, hires were little changed and total separations were unchanged at 5.1 million each. Within separations, both quits (3.2 million) and layoffs and discharges (1.7 million) were little changed.
emphasis added
The following graph shows job openings (black line), hires (dark blue), Layoff, Discharges and other (red column), and Quits (light blue column) from the JOLTS.

This series started in December 2000.

Note: The difference between JOLTS hires and separations is similar to the CES (payroll survey) net jobs headline numbers. This report is for November; the employment report to be released on Friday will be for December.

Click on graph for larger image.

Note that hires (dark blue) and total separations (red and light blue columns stacked) are usually pretty close each month. This is a measure of labor market turnover.  When the blue line is above the two stacked columns, the economy is adding net jobs - when it is below the columns, the economy is losing jobs.

The spike in layoffs and discharges in March 2020 is labeled, but off the chart to better show the usual data.

Jobs openings decreased in November to 7.15 million from 7.45 million in October.

The number of job openings (black) were down 11% year-over-year. 

Quits were up 4% year-over-year. These are voluntary separations. (See light blue columns at bottom of graph for trend for "quits").
- ADP: Private Employment Increased 41,000 in December — From ADP: ADP National Employment Report: Private Sector Employment Increased by 41,000 Jobs in December; Annual Pay was Up 4.4%
“Small establishments recovered from November job losses with positive end-of-year hiring, even as large employers pulled back,” said Dr. Nela Richardson, chief economist, ADP.
emphasis added
This was below the consensus forecast of 50,000 jobs added. The BLS will report on Friday, and the consensus is for 55,000 jobs added.

Since the overall participation rate is impacted by both cyclical (recession) and demographic (aging population, younger people staying in school) reasons, here is the employment-population ratio for the key working age group: 25 to 54 years old.

The 25 to 54 years old participation rate was unchanged in December at 83.8%% from 83.8% in November.

The 25 to 54 employment population ratio increased to 80.7% from 80.6% the previous month.

Both are down slightly from the recent peaks, but still near the highest level this millennium.

Average Hourly Wages

The graph shows the nominal year-over-year change in "Average Hourly Earnings" for all private employees from the Current Employment Statistics (CES).  

There was a huge increase at the beginning of the pandemic as lower paid employees were let go, and then the pandemic related spike reversed a year later.

Wage growth has trended down after peaking at 5.9% YoY in March 2022 and was at 3.8% YoY in December, up from 3.6% YoY in November. 

Part Time for Economic Reasons

From the BLS report:
"The number of people employed part time for economic reasons, at 5.3 million, changed little in December but is up by 980,000 over the year. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs."
The number of persons working part time for economic reasons decreased in December to 5.34 million from 5.49 million in November.  This is well above the pre-pandemic levels and near the highest levels since mid-2021.

These workers are included in the alternate measure of labor underutilization (U-6) that decreased to 8.4% from 8.7% in November. This is down from the record high in April 2020 of 22.9% and up from the lowest level on record (seasonally adjusted) in December 2022 (6.6%). (This series started in 1994). This measure is well above the 7.0% level in February 2020 (pre-pandemic).

Unemployed over 26 Weeks

This graph shows the number of workers unemployed for 27 weeks or more.

According to the BLS, there are 1.95 million workers who have been unemployed for more than 26 weeks and still want a job, up from 1.91 million in November.

This is down from post-pandemic high of 4.171 million, and up from the recent low of 1.056 million.

This is above pre-pandemic levels.

Summary:

The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000.  The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

This was another weak employment report.

articles.title: December Employment Preview
articles.description:
On Friday at 8:30 AM ET, the BLS will release the employment report for December. The consensus is for 55,000 jobs added, and for the unemployment rate to decrease to 4.5%. There were 64,000 jobs added in November, and the unemployment rate was at 4.6%.

From Goldman Sachs:
We forecast that payrolls rose 70k (vs. 55k consensus) in December and the unemployment rate fell to 4.5% (vs. 4.5% consensus). ... We expect the unemployment rate to edge down to 4.5% because the increase to 4.6% in November largely reflected the impact of furloughed federal government workers during the shutdown.
emphasis added
From BofA:
Dec NFP are likely to tick up to a stable 70k (private: 75k) print, higher than consensus expectations. Initial claims remain low and continuing claims have trended lower since Oct. Education & health jobs should remain the driver of payroll growth. Given the strength in air travel and holiday spending, we project a rise in leisure & hospitality jobs. After the u-rate jumping to 4.6% in Nov, in part due to shutdown-related distortions, we expect a decline to 4.5%. It is likely that the worst is behind us in the labor market.
• ADP Report: The ADP employment report showed 41,000 private sector jobs were added in December.  This was slightly below consensus forecasts.  However, in general, ADP hasn't been very useful in forecasting the BLS report.

• ISM Surveys: Note that the ISM indexes are diffusion indexes based on the number of firms hiring (not the number of hires).  The ISM® manufacturing employment index increased to 44.9%, up from 44.0% the previous month. This suggests manufacturing jobs lost in December. The ADP report indicated 5,000 manufacturing jobs lost in December.

The ISM® services employment index increased to 52.0%, up from 48.9%.  This suggests job gains in December.  

• Unemployment Claims: The weekly claims report showed about the same number of initial unemployment claims during the reference week at 224,000 in December compared to 222,000 in November.  This suggests about the same number of layoffs in December as in November.

• Conclusion: Over the last 6 months, employment gains averaged 17 thousand per month.  The ADP report, the ISM Surveys, and unemployment claims suggest similar gains in December compared to November.   I'll take the over for December - but still weak hiring.

articles.title: BLS: Job Openings Declined to 7.1 million in November
articles.description:
From the BLS: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Summary
The number of job openings was little changed at 7.1 million in November, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Over the month, hires were little changed and total separations were unchanged at 5.1 million each. Within separations, both quits (3.2 million) and layoffs and discharges (1.7 million) were little changed.
emphasis added
The following graph shows job openings (black line), hires (dark blue), Layoff, Discharges and other (red column), and Quits (light blue column) from the JOLTS.

This series started in December 2000.

Note: The difference between JOLTS hires and separations is similar to the CES (payroll survey) net jobs headline numbers. This report is for November; the employment report to be released on Friday will be for December.

Click on graph for larger image.

Note that hires (dark blue) and total separations (red and light blue columns stacked) are usually pretty close each month. This is a measure of labor market turnover.  When the blue line is above the two stacked columns, the economy is adding net jobs - when it is below the columns, the economy is losing jobs.

The spike in layoffs and discharges in March 2020 is labeled, but off the chart to better show the usual data.

Jobs openings decreased in November to 7.15 million from 7.45 million in October.

The number of job openings (black) were down 11% year-over-year. 

Quits were up 4% year-over-year. These are voluntary separations. (See light blue columns at bottom of graph for trend for "quits").

clusters.headline: Wholesale Used Car Prices Increased Slightly in December; Up 0.4% Year-over-year
clusters.briefing:
- Wholesale Used Car Prices Increased Slightly in December; Up 0.4% Year-over-year — From Manheim Consulting today: Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index: December 2025 Trends
The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index (MUVVI) rose to 205.5, reflecting a 0.4% increase for wholesale used-vehicle prices (adjusted for mix, mileage, and seasonality) compared to December 2024. The December index is up 0.1% month over month.
emphasis added
Click on graph for larger image.

This index from Manheim Consulting is based on all completed sales transactions at Manheim’s U.S. auctions.

The Manheim index suggests used car prices increased in December (seasonally adjusted) and were up 0.4% YoY.
- Light Vehicle Sales Increased to 16.0 Million SAAR in December — The BEA reported that light vehicle sales were at 16.0 million in December on a seasonally adjusted annual basis (SAAR). This was up 1.9% from the sales rate in November, and down 4.9% from December 2024.

Click on graph for larger image.

This graph shows light vehicle sales since 2006 from the BEA (blue) through December.

Vehicle sales were over 17 million SAAR in March and April as consumers rushed to "beat the tariffs".

Then sales were depressed in May and June. 

Sales were boosted in August and September due to the termination of the EV credit at the end of September.

The second graph shows light vehicle sales since the BEA started keeping data in 1967.

Sales in Decvember were slightly above the consensus forecast.

Light vehicle sales were up 2.4% in 2025 compared to 2024.
- Heavy Truck Sales Collapsed in Q4; Down 32.5% Year-over-year in December — This graph shows heavy truck sales since 1967 using data from the BEA. The dashed line is the December 2025 seasonally adjusted annual sales rate (SAAR) of 311 thousand.

Note: "Heavy trucks - trucks more than 14,000 pounds gross vehicle weight."

Click on graph for larger image.

Heavy truck sales were at 311 thousand SAAR in December, down from 336 thousand in November, and down 32.5% from 461 thousand SAAR in December 2024.

Sales were down 15.3% in 2025 compared to annual sales in 2024.

Usually, heavy truck sales decline sharply prior to a recession, and sales have collapsed recently.

For manufacturing, the December Industrial Production report and the January New York and Philly Fed manufacturing surveys will be released.

No major economic releases scheduled.

6:00 AM: NFIB Small Business Optimism Index for December.

8:30 AM: The Consumer Price Index for December from the BLS. The consensus is for 0.3% increase in CPI, and a 0.3% increase in core CPI.  The consensus is for CPI to be up 2.7% year-over-year and core CPI to be up 2.7% YoY.

10:00 AM: New Home Sales for September and October from the Census Bureau.

8:30 AM ET: The Producer Price Index for December from the BLS. The consensus is for a 0.3% increase in PPI, and a 0.2% increase in core PPI.

8:30 AM: Retail sales for November is scheduled to be released.  

The consensus is for a 0.4% increase in retail sales.

This graph shows retail sales since 1992. 

This is monthly retail sales and food service, seasonally adjusted (total and ex-gasoline).

December retail sales for December have not been scheduled yet.

10:00 AM: Existing Home Sales for December from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). The consensus is for 4.23 million SAAR, up from 4.13 million.

The graph shows existing home sales from 1994 through the report last month.

2:00 PM: the Federal Reserve Beige Book, an informal review by the Federal Reserve Banks of current economic conditions in their Districts.

----- Thursday, January 15th -----

8:30 AM: The New York Fed Empire State manufacturing survey for January. The consensus is for a reading of 1.0, down from -3.9.

The consensus is for a 0.2% increase in Industrial Production, and for Capacity Utilization to be unchanged at 76.0%.

Economic activity in the services sector continued to expand in December, say the nation’s purchasing and supply executives in the latest ISM® Services PMI® Report. The Services PMI® registered at 54.4 percent, finishing 2025 on a positive note with its 10th month in expansion territory — and its highest reading — of the year.

The report was issued today by Steve Miller, CPSM, CSCP, Chair of the Institute for Supply Management® (ISM®) Services Business Survey Committee:

“In December, the Services PMI® registered a reading of 54.4 percent, 1.8 percentage points higher than the November figure of 52.6 percent and a third consecutive month of expansion. The Business Activity Index continued in expansion territory in December, registering 56 percent, 1.5 percentage points higher than the reading of 54.5 percent recorded in November. The New Orders Index also remained in expansion in December, with a reading of 57.9 percent, 5 percentage points above November’s figure of 52.9 percent. The Employment Index expanded for the first time in seven months with a reading of 52 percent, a 3.1-percentage point improvement from the 48.9 percent recorded in November — the fifth consecutive monthly increase since a reading of 46.4 percent in July.

“The Supplier Deliveries Index registered 51.8 percent, 2.3 percentage points lower than the 54.1 percent recorded in November. This is the 13th consecutive month that the index has been in expansion territory, indicating slower supplier delivery performance. (Supplier Deliveries is the only ISM® PMI® Reports index that is inversed; a reading of above 50 percent indicates slower deliveries, which is typical as the economy improves and customer demand increases.)

“The Prices Index registered 64.3 percent in December, its lowest level since a reading of 60.9 percent in March 2025. The December figure was a 1.1-percentage point drop from November’s reading of 65.4 percent. The index has exceeded 60 percent for 13 straight months.br /> emphasis added
Employment expanded following six consecutive month of contraction.

articles.title: Schedule for Week of January 11, 2026
articles.description:
The key reports this week are December CPI, Existing Home Sales and November Retail Sales. Also, New Home Sales for September and October will be released.

For manufacturing, the December Industrial Production report and the January New York and Philly Fed manufacturing surveys will be released.

----- Monday, January 12th -----

No major economic releases scheduled.

----- Tuesday, January 13th -----

6:00 AM: NFIB Small Business Optimism Index for December.

8:30 AM: The Consumer Price Index for December from the BLS. The consensus is for 0.3% increase in CPI, and a 0.3% increase in core CPI.  The consensus is for CPI to be up 2.7% year-over-year and core CPI to be up 2.7% YoY.

10:00 AM: New Home Sales for September and October from the Census Bureau.

This graph shows New Home Sales since 1963 through August 2025.

The dashed line is the sales rate for August.

The consensus is for 714 thousand SAAR for October.

----- Wednesday, January 14th -----

7:00 AM ET: The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) will release the results for the mortgage purchase applications index. This will be two weeks of data.

8:30 AM ET: The Producer Price Index for December from the BLS. The consensus is for a 0.3% increase in PPI, and a 0.2% increase in core PPI.

8:30 AM: Retail sales for November is scheduled to be released.  

The consensus is for a 0.4% increase in retail sales.

This graph shows retail sales since 1992. 

This is monthly retail sales and food service, seasonally adjusted (total and ex-gasoline).

December retail sales for December have not been scheduled yet.

10:00 AM: Existing Home Sales for December from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). The consensus is for 4.23 million SAAR, up from 4.13 million.

The graph shows existing home sales from 1994 through the report last month.

2:00 PM: the Federal Reserve Beige Book, an informal review by the Federal Reserve Banks of current economic conditions in their Districts.

----- Thursday, January 15th -----

8:30 AM: The initial weekly unemployment claims report will be released.  The consensus is for 208K, unchanged from 208K.

8:30 AM: The New York Fed Empire State manufacturing survey for January. The consensus is for a reading of 1.0, down from -3.9.

8:30 AM: the Philly Fed manufacturing survey for January.  The consensus is for a reading of -5.0, up from -10.2.
----- Friday, January 16th -----

9:15 AM: The Fed will release Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization for December.

This graph shows industrial production since 1967.

The consensus is for a 0.2% increase in Industrial Production, and for Capacity Utilization to be unchanged at 76.0%.

10:00 AM: The January NAHB homebuilder survey. 

The consensus is for a reading of 40, up from 39 the previous month. Any number below 50 indicates that more builders view sales conditions as poor than good.

clusters.headline: MBA: Mortgage Applications Decreased Over a Two-Week Period
clusters.briefing: From the MBA: MMortgage Applications Decreased Over a Two-Week Period in Latest MBA Weekly Survey Mortgage applications decreased 9.7 percent from two weeks earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Weekly Mortgage Applications Survey for the week ending January 2, 2026. The results include an adjustment for the holidays. The Market Composite Index, a measure of mortgage loan application volume, decreased 9.7 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis from two weeks earlier. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 28 percent compared with two weeks ago. The holiday adjusted Refinance Index decreased 14 percent from two weeks ago and was 133 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The unadjusted Refinance Index decreased 31 percent from two weeks ago and was 108 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index decreased 6 percent from two weeks earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 23 percent compared with two weeks ago and was 10 percent higher than the same week one year ago . “Mortgage rates started the New Year with a decline to 6.25 percent, the lowest level since September 2024. Refinance applications were up 7 percent for the week but were at a slower pace than in the weeks leading up to the holidays,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist. “FHA refinance applications saw a 19 percent increase, although that was a partial rebound from a drop the week before. MBA continues to expect mortgage rates to stay around current levels, with spells of refinance opportunities in the weeks when rates move lower.” Added Kan, “Purchase applications were 10 percent higher than the same week a year ago but were down over the week following decreases in conventional and FHA applications. The average loan size was $408,700, the smallest in a year, driven by lower average loan sizes across both conventional and government loan types.” ... From the MBA: MMortgage Applications Decreased Over a Two-Week Period in Latest MBA Weekly Survey
Mortgage applications decreased 9.7 percent from two weeks earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Weekly Mortgage Applications Survey for the week ending January 2, 2026. The results include an adjustment for the holidays.

The Market Composite Index, a measure of mortgage loan application volume, decreased 9.7 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis from two weeks earlier. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 28 percent compared with two weeks ago. The holiday adjusted Refinance Index decreased 14 percent from two weeks ago and was 133 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The unadjusted Refinance Index decreased 31 percent from two weeks ago and was 108 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index decreased 6 percent from two weeks earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 23 percent compared with two weeks ago and was 10 percent higher than the same week one year ago.

“Mortgage rates started the New Year with a decline to 6.25 percent, the lowest level since September 2024. Refinance applications were up 7 percent for the week but were at a slower pace than in the weeks leading up to the holidays,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist. “FHA refinance applications saw a 19 percent increase, although that was a partial rebound from a drop the week before. MBA continues to expect mortgage rates to stay around current levels, with spells of refinance opportunities in the weeks when rates move lower.”

Added Kan, “Purchase applications were 10 percent higher than the same week a year ago but were down over the week following decreases in conventional and FHA applications. The average loan size was $408,700, the smallest in a year, driven by lower average loan sizes across both conventional and government loan types.”

clusters.briefing: DENVER--(BUSINESS WIRE)--NUBURU, Inc. (NYSE American: BURU) (“NUBURU” o la “Società”), una piattaforma integrata di nuova generazione per la difesa e la sicurezza a duplice impiego, oggi ha annunciato di aver completato l’acquisizione del 70% del capitale di controllo di Tekne S.p.A. (“Tekne”) tramite la propria società controllata NUBURU Defense LLC. Il closing notarile è stato perfezionato oggi in Italia, successivamente all’autorizzazione Golden Power concessa dal governo italiano il 5 agost
